item.title: A Meteorite Found in the Sahara Is a 4.1-Billion-Year-Old Piece of Mars
item.description: Minerals in the space rock provide hints about the early history of the red planet, when water was flowing on the surface.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: As Picard on ‘Star Trek’, Patrick Stewart Influenced Generations of Scientists
item.description: Stewart’s iconic “Star Trek” character inspired astronomers and astronauts in countless ways: “You were the captain of my childhood,” one astrophysicist said.
item.dc:creator: Robin George Andrews
item.media:description: Patrick Stewart in 1990 as Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the U.S.S. Enterprise in “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”

item.title: Dozens of Headless Skeletons Pose a Macabre Mystery
item.description: Mass graves found at a Stone Age farming settlement in Slovakia have researchers baffled about the details — including the location of the missing skulls.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz

item.title: The New DNA Technology That Linked Ted Bundy to a 52-Year-Old Cold Case
item.description: Software known as STRmix was instrumental in identifying Mr. Bundy’s DNA in a decades-old sample.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Nazaryan
item.media:description: Ted Bundy, one of the nation’s most prolific and notorious spree killers, on trial for murder in a Miami courtroom in 1979.

item.title: Three Stone Age Caves Reveal Continual Cannibalism
item.description: A tour of the three caves in southern Spain suggests that people in the area cannibalized one another as funerary practice over many generations.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Rapp Learn

item.title: After Reinventing Mathematics, Can A.I. Eradicate Computer Bugs?
item.description: Using the same techniques that allowed A.I. technologies to crack a million-dollar math problem, researchers are building new systems that aim to solve the world’s cybersecurity crisis.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times
item.media:description: An in-progress “software verification” of a large codebase, demonstrated at the headquarters of the start-up &Truth in Palo Alto, Calif.

item.title: These Patients Struggle With Runaway Bones. Finally There’s Hope.
item.description: F.O.P., a rare genetic condition, causes uncontrolled explosions of bone. New drugs may slow or halt the process.
item.dc:creator: Stella Raine Chu
item.media:credit: KT Kanazawich for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jordyn Bugarin, who lives with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, or F.O.P., a rare genetic disorder that slowly turns muscle and connective tissue into bone, was in a clinical trial for a monoclonal antibody treatment for the condition.

item.title: After Flying Past the Moon, an Artemis II Astronaut Lands at a New Job in California
item.description: Reid Wiseman, now a retired emeritus astronaut, will become deputy director of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, NASA’s premier center for deep-space robotic missions.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: Reid Wiseman will become deputy director of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.

item.title: Can Scientists Make Football Safer?
item.description: Researchers are exploring novel ways to treat, even prevent, the brain disease C.T.E. One of the most surprising: near-infrared light.
item.dc:creator: Lynne Peeples
item.media:credit: Kim Raff for The New York Times

item.title: Doctors in Ukraine Try Treating Infections Like Biological Warfare Attacks
item.description: As many as 40 percent of injured soldiers face severe infections that can lead to amputations and death. One initiative is trying to fix that.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata and Marc Santora
item.media:credit: Johanna-Maria Fritz for The New York Times
item.media:description: Hailie Uren, a clinical pharmacologist, measured a patient’s blood pressure in Dnipro, Ukraine, last month.

item.title: That Mummy for Sale on Facebook Could Make You Ill
item.description: Experts warn that online black markets for mummified remains could pose health risks.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz

item.title: Scary Ghost Stories From New York Times Archives
item.description: From haunted zoo cages to ghostly bar owners, here are five stories from our archives that will make you shiver, or maybe chuckle.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Bahr

item.title: A Marathon Runner’s Hard Lesson
item.description: Racing in Chicago showed your newsletter host firsthand how warming is disrupting the sport.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles
item.media:description: Temperatures approached 80 degrees Fahrenheit during this year’s Chicago marathon.

item.title: New Batteries That Store Blistering Heat Are Taking Off
item.description: Large batteries that store electricity have revolutionized power grids and car markets. Now some start-ups are betting that “heat batteries” could be just as transformative.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:credit: Tim Gruber for The New York Times
item.media:description: Thermal batteries like these in Big Stone City, S.D., can store and provide heat for industrial purposes.

item.title: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
item.description: In a unilateral declaration by the health secretary, several injections promoted by online influencers will become widely available. The F.D.A. had advised against the move.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.media:description: Peptides are short chains of amino acids that give the body basic instructions. While the F.D.A. has approved some peptide compounds, such as insulin to manage diabetes, many others lack scientific evidence of efficacy or safety.

item.title: Brain Disease Is Pervasive in N.F.L., New Estimate Suggests
item.description: Using statistical techniques, a new study has arrived at a harrowing estimate: Three of four retired pro football players most likely had C.T.E. at death.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson and John Branch

item.title: U.S. Restricts Trade With Chinese Genomics Company
item.description: The move will block shipments from BGI, a major Chinese firm that U.S. officials allege is associated with forced labor and the abuse of minority groups.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Robbins and Ana Swanson
item.media:description: A BGI exhibit in Beijing last year. The Trump administration added the company, a major Chinese genomics company that U.S. officials have long eyed with suspicion, to a trade blacklist aimed at barring products made with forced labor in China.

item.title: Trump Administration Backs Down on an Opioid Ban After Kratom Industry Lobbying
item.description: Health officials will now allow some levels of a powerful substance to remain in products marketed as natural. The change could help a G.O.P. donor facing wrongful death lawsuits.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.media:credit: Nick Oxford for The New York Times
item.media:description: Banners promoting the sale of kratom products outside a smoke shop in Tulsa, Okla., earlier this year.

item.title: A New Dwarf Planet (Probably) Spotted Beyond Pluto
item.description: The object, known for now as 2026 ED138, is one of the first discoveries by the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: E.P.A. Loosens Methane Rules for Oil Firms
item.description: The Biden administration had sought to crack down on methane leaks, a big driver of climate change. Those rules are now being scaled back.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:description: An oil drilling operation in Carlsbad, N.M.

item.title: Nanotyrannus Skeleton ‘Jodi’ Is Auctioned for $47.3 Million
item.description: The T. Rex cousin is the latest dinosaur fossil to fetch a high price at an auction, this time at Sotheby’s.
item.dc:creator: Sopan Deb
item.media:description: Scientists long debated whether Nanotyrannus was from a separate group of Tyrannosaur species, or if they were teen specimens of T. rex. The separate group hypothesis has recently prevailed.

item.title: Did the Hardest A.I. Problem Just Get Much Easier?
item.description: A prominent researcher claims to have a revolutionary approach to “interpretability,” or the science of why A.I. models do what they do. Other experts aren’t so sure.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz

item.title: Antidepressants Don’t Correct A Chemical Imbalance. How, Then, Do They Work?
item.description: Here’s how psychiatrists like me think about the most promising hypotheses.
item.dc:creator: Awais Aftab

item.title: It’s Docktober. Do You Know Where the Sea Slugs Are?
item.description: Where there are floating docks, there are often communities of colorful marine organisms just below — and a community of curious people just above.
item.dc:creator: Chona Kasinger and Alan Burdick
item.media:credit: Chona Kasinger for The New York Times

item.title: The Science Behind Your Reaction to Art
item.description: The Honolulu Museum of Art is showing how art can influence thinking, perspective and mood, in an exhibition that is part of a trend by museums to mix science and art.
item.dc:creator: Michael Janofsky

item.title: Gaze at the Cosmic Dawn in Dizzying Detail
item.description: A new simulation offers a highly immersive look at what happened during the first couple of billion years following the Big Bang.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller
item.category: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (Journal)

item.title: Neutrinos Are Everywhere. A Physicist Explains.
item.description: Dr. Francis Halzen, the recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics, sheds some light on the mysterious, subatomic particles that whiz through us every day.
item.dc:creator: Steven Kurutz
item.media:description: “I still have both feet on the ground,” said Francis Halzen, who has made a lifelong study of elusive neutrinos.

item.title: Shiny Glass Skyscrapers Are a Hot Thing. Literally.
item.description: They’re transforming cities with million-dollar views and a message of modernity. But climate change makes cooling them tricky and costly.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan, Zunaira Saieed and Mira Rojanasakul
item.category: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat

item.title: What Happened to the Neanderthals?
item.description: Scientists now know that they shared many of the sophisticated abilities of Homo sapiens. So why are we the only humans left standing?
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson
